I’ve been farming these lands in Quzhou County for over fifty years, and I know the North China Plain like the back of my hand. At seventy-three, I don’t have the strength I once did, but my experience and schooling mean I understand the science behind the soil. I still hold six mu of good irrigated land, and I see no reason to change what works: the winter wheat–summer maize double-cropping system is the backbone of our county, and it fits the climate and the market. My winter wheat was sown last October and is starting to green up now, so my immediate job is to nurse it through to harvest in early June. Right after the combine leaves the wheat field, I will plant summer maize without delay—every day counts in the short summer season. I use improved varieties for both crops because the county seed station recommends them and they give stable yields. I keep my fertilizer rates moderate but balanced; I’ve learned that piling on nitrogen only burns money and damages the soil. I will rotary-till the maize field after wheat harvest because it controls weeds and breaks up the stubble quickly without exhausting me. For irrigation, I will give the wheat three good waterings from now until grain filling, and the maize one critical irrigation at the jointing stage if the summer rains are stingy. Two pesticide applications on each crop are enough if I time them right—one for the main disease and one for the main pest. I expect around 550 kg per mu for the wheat and 650 kg per mu for the maize if the weather cooperates.
